sources.news_title: Nvidia shares fall despite bumper earnings
sources.text:
Nvidia shares dipped Wednesday after its bumper earnings failed to quell jitters over Jensen Huang’s departure, as its new leadership launched a charm offensive to win over skeptical employees and investors.
In addition to increasing stock buybacks, Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress reportedly promised pay raises Wednesday in the chipmaker’s first employee town hall following Huang’s ouster, amid concerns the shake-up could drive a talent exodus; Kress added that the firm’s “passion to innovate” would not change.
The saga has laid bare a divide between Silicon Valley and DC, a former politico-turned-tech executive told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman: “Out here, the question is whether Jensen will be back at Nvidia by Christmas… In Washington, it’s whether he’s going to prison.”

sources.news_title: Nvidia Shares Retreat as Strong Earnings Fail to Resolve Leadership Uncertainty
sources.text:
Nov. 18 — Nvidia shares reversed early gains on Wednesday, dragging several artificial intelligence-related stocks lower as investors remained uneasy about the chipmaker’s future following the abrupt departure of co-founder Jensen Huang.
The retreat came despite a stronger-than-expected earnings report and an upbeat revenue outlook, which initially lifted sentiment across the technology sector. The market reaction suggests that robust demand for Nvidia’s AI chips has not been enough to overcome concerns about leadership, regulatory scrutiny and the company’s influence over the broader AI ecosystem.
Nvidia shares fell nearly 2% after gaining as much as 3% in premarket trading. If sustained, the decline would erase more than $80 billion in market value, adding to approximately $2 trillion lost between the company’s October record and Tuesday’s close.
The technology-focused Nasdaq-100 has shed roughly $1.94 trillion in market value so far in November as investors reassess elevated AI valuations amid concerns about China, data center spending and tighter regulation.
“We believe yesterday’s results have stabilized sentiment and put a floor under the recent AI selloff, but they have postponed rather than permanently cured investor anxiety,” said Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint.
Strong Results Offer Only Temporary Relief
Nvidia’s latest financial performance demonstrated that demand for its advanced processors remains exceptionally strong.
Third-quarter revenue more than doubled year over year to $115.84 billion, marking the company’s 17th consecutive quarter of beating analyst estimates, according to LSEG data.
Its fourth-quarter revenue forecast also exceeded Wall Street expectations. Management raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to approximately 75%, saying demand continued to exceed available supply.
Adjusted gross margin reached 74.9%. Nvidia expects margins to decline to between 71% and 72% this quarter as higher supply costs take effect, before recovering to between 72% and 73% in fiscal 2028.
The results provided evidence that the leadership upheaval has not yet disrupted Nvidia’s product roadmap or weakened demand for its chips.
However, investors remain concerned about the company’s ability to maintain its competitive position under new leadership.
“Strong earnings have bought management time,” said Saxo strategist Charu Chanana.
Leadership Uncertainty Continues to Weigh on Shares
Nvidia’s leadership transition remains a central concern for investors.
Chairman Harvey Jones has ruled out reinstating Huang despite his offer to return. The board has appointed executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search for a permanent chief executive, considering both internal and external candidates.
Interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has described the situation as “business as usual,” pointing to continued support from customers and suppliers.
Nevertheless, HSBC analysts said Nvidia shares could struggle to recover until the company appoints a permanent chief executive and demonstrates that its new leadership can execute planned product launches.
The company is also facing an independent investigation and a Wall Street Journal report that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating it. These developments have added another layer of uncertainty to an already volatile AI investment environment.
China Sales Disappear From Nvidia’s Forecast
Nvidia’s exposure to China remains another important issue for investors.
The company generated $2.4 billion in licensed Hopper data center chip sales to China during the third quarter. However, its latest forecast assumes no further shipments of those products to the country.
Management said the outlook reflects existing U.S. export controls and confirmed that Nvidia is no longer shipping those products to China.
The company expects demand from other markets to absorb the loss of Chinese sales, although executives are still evaluating aspects of the new export restrictions announced by the Trump administration.
Christopher Brown, vice president of investments at Synovus, which holds Nvidia shares, said Kress provided confident responses regarding the restrictions and demand from other markets.
“We just need to understand that demand is not the same as legal ability to ship,” Brown said.
The distinction highlights a significant challenge for Nvidia: strong global demand does not automatically translate into sales when government restrictions limit where advanced chips can be delivered.
Anthropic IPO Becomes Another Test for AI Investors
The next major test for the AI sector is Anthropic’s anticipated public offering, which is expected to be priced later Wednesday.
The offering could value the AI company at as much as $1.4 trillion, potentially intensifying competition for investor capital among established technology companies and emerging AI businesses.
The broader AI trade has already faced pressure from concerns about expensive valuations, massive data center investments and uncertainty over the returns from artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Nvidia’s retreat, despite its strong earnings, illustrates the market’s growing distinction between demand for AI technology and confidence in the companies financing and supplying its expansion.
For now, Nvidia’s financial performance remains strong. But until its leadership transition, regulatory challenges and China exposure become clearer, investors may remain reluctant to fully restore their confidence in the chipmaker and the wider AI rally.

sources.news_title: Nvidia tops estimates with $115.8B quarter, guides Q4 to $132.6B
sources.text:
Nvidia tops estimates with $115.8B quarter, guides Q4 to $132.6B
Nvidia beat estimates with $115.8B fiscal Q3 revenue and guided Q4 to $132.6B in its first report since Jensen Huang's exit, with $227.3B left in buybacks.
Nvidia (NVDA) beat Wall Street estimates on both lines in its fiscal third quarter, reporting $115.8 billion in revenue against a $108.8 billion consensus after the market closed on November 17.
The company said in its earnings release that data center revenue of $107.6 billion came in ahead of a $101.9 billion estimate, and that diluted earnings of $2.68 a share topped a $2.47 forecast. Gross margin was 74.8%, down 20 basis points from the prior quarter and up 140 basis points from a year earlier.
First results without Huang
These are the first results Nvidia has filed since co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive earlier in November after personal controversies that shook the stock. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who has held the finance role since 2013, is leading the company while the board searches for a permanent successor, a search that began alongside an independent board probe into the disclosures around Huang’s conduct.
“Our momentum is real,” Kress said in the release, adding that Vera Rubin, the company’s next data-center platform, is “off to an explosive start.”
Guidance and buybacks point past the crisis
Nvidia guided fourth-quarter revenue to a range of $127.4 billion to $132.6 billion, above the $125.3 billion consensus. The company returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter through buybacks and dividends and said $227.3 billion remained available under its repurchase authorization.
The investigations Nvidia’s numbers do not settle
The quarter closed amid federal scrutiny. The New York Times reported in October that US intelligence agencies were surveilling Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset with ties to the former chief executive. Megaspeed International, the cloud provider at the center of the reports, said on November 15 that it is conducting an internal investigation and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025. An Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the surveillance reports, saying the company is confident the US government would alert it to any threat to American industry.
The Departments of Commerce and Justice issued a joint statement on the Megaspeed investigation on November 17, the same day Nvidia reported.
Shares rose 2.4% in after-hours trading from a $155.32 close. The stock had fallen 32% from early October and had declined for six straight weeks, Nvidia’s longest losing streak since 2012.

sources.news_title: After the AI Sell-Off: Who Actually Gets Rich? - FINCHANNEL
sources.text:
Nvidia has just reported the best quarter in its history. Its shares did not care. Why record numbers can no longer rescue the stock and what could change that.
On Tuesday evening, New York time, Nvidia published results that any company in the world would envy. Revenue for the quarter that ended on 25 October reached $115.8 billion, more than double a year earlier. Net profit was $65.3 billion, in three months. The company told investors to expect $130 billion in the current quarter, and raised its growth outlook for next year from 70% to 75%.
by Dr. Gil Feiler
The shares rose about 5% in after-hours trading. By the time markets opened on Wednesday morning, the gain had gone, and at the time of writing the stock was trading slightly below Tuesday’s close.
That gap between the numbers and the share price is the real story of this sell-off. It tells us that the question investors are asking about artificial intelligence has changed, and that a better quarterly report cannot answer it.
The largest loss of value in market history
On 6 October, Nvidia closed at a record, valued at about $5.8 trillion, the most valuable company on earth. Six weeks later its shares had fallen about 35%, and roughly $2 trillion of market value had disappeared. Fortune described it as the biggest dollar drop in so short a period in the history of capital markets. No company has ever lost so much value so quickly, because no company has ever been worth so much.
The fall came in waves. On 5 November, the day after the US midterm elections, Nvidia lost 9.3% and about $448 billion in a single session, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%. A week later, on 12 November, the company announced that Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it for 33 years, had resigned as chief executive and left the board. The shares fell as much as 14% that morning before recovering part of the loss. By the close of 13 November, Nvidia had lost $573 billion in one week, its largest weekly loss on record according to Dow Jones Market Data, and its value had dropped below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025. Apple has overtaken it as the world’s most valuable company.
Nvidia was not alone. Chipmakers, memory producers, data-centre operators and the so-called neoclouds that rent out AI computing power all fell together. But Nvidia is the measure of the AI trade, and its fall is the measure of the change in mood.
What the results actually said
It is worth being precise, because the business and the share price have moved in opposite directions.
Data-centre revenue, the heart of the AI business, was $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year ago. Gross margin was 74.8%, a level most manufacturers never see. The company returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter and still has about $227 billion of buyback authority left. Its supply and capacity commitments have reached $390 billion, a sign that it expects demand to continue. And its outlook for the coming quarter assumes no data-centre computing sales in China at all.
“Our momentum is real,” said Colette Kress, the finance chief who is now interim chief executive. On the evidence of the numbers, she is right. Nvidia remains an excellent company. The share now trades at about 12 times expected earnings for the next twelve months, the lowest multiple since 2012, according to LSEG data reported by Reuters. By that measure it has rarely been cheaper.
So why did the shares not respond?
Why good numbers no longer move the price
First, the question has moved from demand to trust. For three years the market asked one thing: will demand for AI chips keep growing? Every quarter Nvidia answered yes, and the shares rose. Today the market is asking different questions. Who will lead the company? What will the board’s investigation and the official inquiries find? Did export-controlled chips reach China, and what will Washington do about it? A quarterly report is evidence about demand. It is not evidence about trust, and it cannot settle questions that are still open.
Second, the politics of AI have changed. After the midterms, resistance to new data centres, which consume enormous amounts of electricity and water, has reached Washington. Every chip Nvidia sells has to be installed in a building that needs permits, power and public consent. If those become harder to obtain, the spending plans of Nvidia’s customers slow down, whatever Nvidia itself reports.
Third, money is no longer cheap. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury note has risen above 5%, and Federal Reserve officials have signalled that further rate rises are possible. A large part of the AI build-out is financed with debt, by data-centre developers and cloud operators whose income lies years in the future. Higher rates hit exactly these projects, and with them the buyers of Nvidia’s chips.
Fourth, and most fundamental: a great company is not the same as a great investment at any price. At its peak, Nvidia’s valuation assumed not only that it would keep growing, but that nothing would go wrong: not in its leadership, not in China, not in politics, not in financing. The price did not leave room for the ordinary misfortunes of business life. When several arrived at once, the market had to reprice risk that it had treated as zero.
Can anything change the picture?
Yes, but probably not the quarterly numbers alone. A strong report is now necessary but not sufficient. Several things could change the mood.
A credible permanent chief executive would matter most. The board says it is considering internal and external candidates and its chairman has said there are no plans to bring Mr Huang back. The market will judge the name, and how quickly it comes.
Clarity on the investigations and on China would remove a large uncertainty. As long as the outcome is unknown, investors will apply a discount, and even good news will be met with suspicion.
Evidence that Nvidia’s customers are earning money from AI, not only spending it, would answer the deeper question behind the whole sector. Estimates of the annual AI revenue needed to justify the infrastructure being built run into the trillions of dollars by the end of the decade. If the revenue appears, the spending is sustainable. If it does not, no chipmaker can grow forever on other companies’ capital budgets.
And finally, interest rates. If inflation eases and rates stop rising, the debt-financed part of the build-out becomes easier to sustain.
Until then, the fall can continue even if the company keeps beating its forecasts. That is uncomfortable, but it is how markets work when the issue is no longer earnings but confidence. A cheaper valuation creates the possibility of recovery; it does not guarantee it. Investors who bought Cisco in 2000, also an excellent company with soaring sales, waited many years to see their purchase price again.
So who actually gets rich?
This is the question I asked in my book Who Gets Rich in the Age of AI, and the sell-off gives a clearer answer than the boom did.
In the boom, the gains went to a small group: the owners of the scarce assets. Nvidia’s early shareholders, its key suppliers, and the handful of firms that could afford to buy the chips. Most workers, and most savers, were not among them, except indirectly, through index funds and pensions that bought more of these stocks the higher they rose.
In the sell-off, the losses are spread far more widely. Index funds weight companies by their market value, so the more Nvidia and its peers rose, the larger the share of an ordinary pension they came to represent. Many savers who never chose to bet on AI found themselves heavily exposed to it. The gains were concentrated; the risk was distributed.
Those who did best were those who did not follow the crowd: investors who took profits, who diversified, or who refused to pay any price for a good story. At our investment house we began reducing our exposure to listed AI stocks around 2023, against the consensus, and we required our analysts to do their own research in the field rather than rely on the same data and models everyone else uses. For a while this cost us relative returns, and it was not a comfortable position. The point is not that we predicted the timing; we did not. The point is that when everyone agrees, the price usually already reflects that agreement, and the risk lies in what nobody is discussing.
There is a wider lesson here, which I develop in The Dictatorship of the Average. AI systems are trained to give the answer most people would give. When investors, analysts and even their algorithms all draw on the same data and the same models, they reach the same conclusions at the same time, and they buy and sell together. The average becomes the ceiling, and the crowd becomes a source of risk rather than safety.
Dr. Gil Feiler is an economist, investor and author based in Tbilisi. He is Advisor to Bank of Georgia, Chairman of the Golden Fleece Real Estate Fund and a Partner at Forest Investment House. His books include Who Gets Rich in the Age of AI: Money, Work, and the Future of the Middle Class and The Dictatorship of the Average: How Artificial Intelligence Turns the Middle into the Ceiling (Beyond Consensus Press).

Quaise Energy has locked down the first customer for its futuristic approach to vaporizing stone and drilling deep into hot rocks for geothermal power. Conveniently, it is also one of the deepest-pocketed and most sophisticated energy buyers on the market today. The market is clearly down with VPPs — in a good way. The capacity of North America’s virtual power plants grew by nearly 26% this year compared to 2025, reaching 47.2 gigawatts of behind-the-meter flexible capacity, according to a new analysis by Wood Mackenzie. “Escalating turbine costs, affordability concerns, and slow supply response to large loads are driving more interest in VPPs,” Elham Akhavan, principal analyst at the consultancy, said in a statement. Residential VPPs alone more than doubled.

Nvidia is making boatloads of cash and confirms Huang is out for good — and I fear the worst for gaming GPUs now
Even Huang himself appears to have admitted defeat at this point
- Nvidia's financial results for Q3 show it has doubled revenue year-on-year
- The board took the time to clarify that Jensen Huang won't be returning
- Huang himself seems to have admitted defeat based on a change in his X profile, and a reported SEC investigation only complicates matters further
Nvidia just revealed some bumper financial results in the wake of the exit of its CEO, and the board has made it clear that Jensen Huang won't be coming back — with the man himself also giving a notable signal that he's given up any hope of that outcome.
Nvidia's fiscal Q3 results saw revenue hit $115.8 billion, which is just over double the money raked in during the same quarter last year, with data center takings accounting for a towering 93% of those earnings.
Colette Kress, interim CEO and the CFO of Nvidia, commented: "Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people."
Obviously that's a reference to Nvidia being the sum of its massed ranks of staff, and not just one person, with the board also making it crystal clear that Jensen Huang won't be returning (as was previously rumored).
Sky News reports that the chairman of the board, Harvey Jones, said in an earnings call that: "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
Huang also appears to be giving up hope that he might return as CEO, an ambition that was doubtless driven by the support he has gained from some quarters built around a petition. Huang even posted on X to say he'd be "honored to answer these calls and return as CEO".
However, the fact that he's just changed his X profile to remove the official Nvidia badge (as spotted by Yahoo Finance) suggests that Huang has accepted that he won't be retaking the helm at Team Green.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Perhaps what might have been the final bucket of cold water to douse Huang's fires of hope is bound up in a report from The Wall Street Journal claiming that the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission) is now investigating Nvidia.
That civil investigation (on top of the FBI looking into this) would further complicate matters, and although the WSJ said the main focus of the probe wasn't clear, it will apparently include the matter of whether Nvidia's disclosures could be judged to have misled investors in the company. This is all theorizing and rumors from anonymous sources, so season liberally.
Analysis: new CEO could heap more woe on PC gamers
We've heard a great deal about the petition and a lot of noise about a possible return for the ex-CEO this week, but what's happened here concludes that particular avenue of speculation – Huang won't be coming back.
Board chairman Jones also commented that Nvidia wants to get a permanent replacement CEO "as quickly as possible", which appears to rule out some kind of internal co-CEO arrangement. (Kress, alongside Ian Buck, who is VP of HPC Computing, has been floated as a possible semi-permanent solution by the rumor mill).
And with the comeback matter effectively at an end, as far as the impact on consumers goes, I think this is bad news for PC gamers. I've argued this point already, and while some have shot back that Huang was hardly in the corner of GeForce GPU buyers anyway — and I fully accept that's a valid point — I still think the alternative is very likely to be worse.
Maybe only slightly worse, granted, but with the RAM crisis set to intensify next year, I'm wary that any new CEO will focus even more on the bottom line — meaning AI and data centers — for the foreseeable future in order to keep the Nvidia ship sailing steadily. And they won't have Huang's fondness for and history with GeForce GPUs, either (which could count for something when it comes to existential discussions about these graphics cards some way down the line, perhaps).
That said, as TechRadar's Editor At Large, Lance Ulanoff, recently pointed out – Huang isn't irreplaceable. And as Colette Kress just made clear, Team Green is the sum of its staff — the 'Nvidians' themselves — not one single leader. But change is coming to Nvidia, and I feel that will inevitably mean a still tighter focus on data center profits at the expense of gaming GPUs (which are already being very much sidelined, as evidenced by some nasty price hikes in recent times).

sources.news_title: Nvidia beats earning expectations, confirms no return for Huang
sources.text:
The much-anticipated Nvidia earnings announcement calmed some market fears with better-than-expected returns and outlook.
Nvidia last night (17 November) reported revenue for the third quarter 2026, of $115.8bn, up 20pc from the previous quarter and up 103pc from a year ago, beating expectations, and reassuring many in the markets after a tumultuous few weeks that saw the departure of its firebrand CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia also said sales would reach some $130bn in the fourth quarter “plus or minus 3pc”, well ahead of analysts’ forecasts.
It was the first outing for Nvidia’s interim CEO and chief financial officer Colette Kress, who was upbeat about the year ahead.
“Our momentum is real,” she said. “Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people. Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.”
She was referring to the Vera Rubin NVL72, what Nvidia describes it as “the most versatile and advanced computing platform ever built”.
“Nvidia’s results show AI demand remains strong,” said Forrester principal analyst Naveen Chhabra.
“More than doubled revenues, software-like margins and guidance remains robust. The bigger question is no longer growth – it’s how long Nvidia can sustain this level of profitability as AI infrastructure scales.”
Chhabra also pointed to the fact that Nvidia did not need China for its success: “Nvidia is proving it can grow without China, at least for now,” he said. “The company’s outlook excludes China data centre compute revenue, highlighting both the strength of global AI demand and the long-term cost of an increasingly fragmented technology landscape.”
The standout metric is margin durability, says Chhabra. “Few companies can double revenue while maintaining gross margins near 75pc,” he said. “Even with guidance moderating to 71pc-72pc, Nvidia continues to operate with profitability levels most technology companies can only aspire to.”
No reprieve for Huang
Huang, who stepped down as CEO on 12 November, released a statement just hours before the earnings announcement describing an “outpouring of calls” from supporters and saying he would be “honoured” to return should the board at Nvidia invite him. However, Nvidia’s board chair made it clear the hunt was on for his successor and there were no plans for a reinstatement of the ousted leader.
Nvidia’s recently appointed – and first ever – board chair Harvey Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” after he “voluntarily resigned”, according to the Financial Times.
As for the future, Forrester’s Chhabra says Nvidia’s next battle is not against competitors alone, but rather a changed landscape.

Huang’s bid on Tuesday to get his job back was the latest twist for the company at the centre of an AI boom that has propelled markets to record highs and boosted global economic growth.
The recent upheaval has battered Nvidia shares—which have lost $700 billion in market value since the scandal broke—and Huang is to be questioned by US lawmakers on December 1 over national security concerns.
A charismatic promoter of AI, his fall triggered immediate calls from Elon Musk and others for his return, and even President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, downplaying the espionage allegations.
• Battle over AI chips –
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said, hours before the earnings release.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
As the spy scandal deepened, Washington on Monday announced new restrictions on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing.
The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which starts this week in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.
The rules also require licenses to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil — countries the US Commerce Department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.
The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.
While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang’s affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.
His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed — a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls.
Investors are watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.
Huang on Tuesday sounded a note of contrition in his statement, saying “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.”

Wall Street shakes again as Nvidia and other jittery AI stocks swing lower
NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. stock market shook again Tuesday as Nvidia and other jittery stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry led widespread losses on Wall Street.
The S&P 500 sank 1% and at one point was on track for its first back-to-back losses of at least 1.5% since March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 848 points, or 1.6%, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.7%.
The center of the action was again Nvidia, which resumed its whipsaw moves. After flipping between modest gains and losses in the morning, it veered lower and dropped as much as 3.7% before trimming the loss down to 0.4%.
The swings came ahead of the chip company’s latest earnings report, which arrived after trading ended for the day and once again came in above analysts’ expectations. It was Nvidia’s first earnings report since interim CEO Colette Kress took over for Jensen Huang, the leather-jacketed star who became one of the most famous faces of the AI boom.” alt=”” />
The pressure is on Kress and Nvidia to show whether the company’s tremendous growth can continue following the stunning resignation of one of AI’s strongest influencers. Nvidia is creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following revelations that Huang had a relationship with an alleged spy for China.
Huang said on the X social-media network Tuesday that he would come back as CEO if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.”
Other AI stocks also swung sharply. Advanced Micro Devices went from an early gain of 1.6% to a drop of 4.7% before trimming its fall to 0.2%. CoreWeave initially climbed 1.8%, flipped to a loss of 6.1% and then finished nearly unchanged.
AI-related stocks have been shaky for months because of a rolling chain of worries. At first, it was concerns that AI stock prices had broadly shot too high in their frenzy. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund further growth. More recently, it was concerns that Democratic victories in this month’s U.S. midterm elections could mean tougher regulations and restrictions on AI data centers.
Such stocks can almost single-handedly set the U.S. market’s course because they’ve grown into some of Wall Street’s most valuable and most influential.
Most of Wall Street was weak Tuesday, as 17 out of every 20 stocks within the index fell,
Home Depot sank 2.4% even though it reported profit for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations.
The retailer has been hampered by a housing market chilled by expensive mortgage rates, which have climbed with Treasury yields because of high oil prices, high inflation and other factors.
The 10-year Treasury yield climbed toward 5.15% Tuesday morning from 5.12% late Monday before later pulling back to 5.10%. It erased its gain after the sharp drops for AI stocks pushed investors to herd into investments seen as safer bets.” alt=”” />
In the morning, yields got support from a report showing better growth in an underlying measure of spending at U.S. retailers than economists expected. Such spending, along with big investments in AI, has helped the U.S. economy continue to grow despite frustration with high inflation.
Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks of banks fell amid concerns about how much pain the broad U.S. economy will feel from any pullback in AI-related spending.
JPMorgan Chase fell 2.4%. A day before, a technical issue at the bank had slowed transactions for customers trying to use the Zelle payment system.
Apple and Marriott had only modest moves following outages in their systems. Apple slipped 0.2%, and Marriott International fell 0.7%.
United Airlines had its own operational struggles, as a system outage forced the carrier to delay departing flights Monday. That came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.
United’s stock lost 4%, but it was also hurt by a rise in oil prices.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 0.8% to $93.14. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.” alt=”” />
The downward momentum on Wall Street was strong enough to erase early gains for The Walt Disney Co. and pull it down 1.5%, even though it reported stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 76.06 points to 7,340.53. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 848.75 to 50,759.42, and the Nasdaq composite sank 181.37 to 24,328.38.
Stock prices generally tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, depending on how interest rates behave. The big businesses across the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer that are nearly 32% higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet.
In stock markets abroad, indexes sank across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 2.6% and dropped to its lowest closing level since February.

sources.news_title: Nvidia shuts door on Jensen Huang comeback hours after he offers to return
sources.text:
Jensen Huang offered to return to Nvidia on Tuesday morning. By evening, Nvidia had answered.
"The NVIDIA board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," chairman Harvey Jones told analysts on the chipmaker's third-quarter earnings call. It was the board's first public response to a growing campaign to return the co-founder to the job he held for 33 years.
Hours earlier, Huang made his case in a post on X. "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," he wrote. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret."
Read More on News
Then he made his offer: "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."
For the first time, the directors who accepted Huang's resignation said on the record what Newsweek had reported Monday, citing Reuters: They are not considering bringing him back.
The refusal came as Nvidia posted a quarter that would ordinarily belong to its founder alone. Revenue reached a record $115.8 billion, up 103 percent from a year earlier, in a quarter that ended October 25, while Huang was still chief executive and days before the scandal that ended his tenure broke.
A Call With One Subject Off Limits
Jones opened Tuesday's call before a single number was read. He said Huang had voluntarily resigned "after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms."
Then he drew a line. "We will not be addressing or taking questions on today's call regarding the circumstances of Jensen's resignation and the ongoing investigation," he said. The board, he added, "will communicate further when appropriate."
Nobody tested it. In roughly 20 minutes of questions from eight analysts, including those at Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, UBS and Goldman Sachs, no one asked about Huang by name. The closest came from Bank of America's Vivek Arya, who asked about talent retention and what "could change during this leadership transition."
Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer and interim chief executive, answered by talking about the company's workforce. Nvidia, she said, would take care of employees during the transition "to make sure that they are safe." She added: "From a business perspective, it's business as usual."
Jones said the board would consider internal and external candidates for the permanent job. The next chief executive, he said, must navigate "advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics."
Security Moves to the Boardroom
In the hours before the call, Nvidia announced a new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. It is a standing board committee that will oversee the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk. Director Suzanne Nora Johnson will chair it, joined by directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri.
Kress also disclosed a quieter retreat from China. Nvidia sold $2.4 billion of licensed Hopper data center chips there in the third quarter. "We are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," she said, and the company's guidance includes none.
Washington is not done with Huang. He has agreed to sit for a transcribed interview with three House committees on December 1, followed by Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter on December 2. Senator Tim Scott, the Republican chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, had separately asked Huang to testify on December 3. Late Tuesday, Huang agreed to appear before the committee, Politico reported. Democrats, poised to take control of Congress after this month's midterm elections, have signaled they will press further. Representative Joe Morelle, a New York Democrat, called the resignation a "wake-up call."
Three Weeks From Denial to Departure
On October 29, The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence had linked Jensen Huang to Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based firm Megaspeed whom some officials suspected of working for China's Ministry of State Security. No publicly disclosed evidence has established that Jensen Huang knowingly assisted Chinese intelligence. China has dismissed the allegations.
On Sunday, November 8, Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a message to employees, and Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation. In its statement that day, the board said it "has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team." That confidence did not last long.
Further reports of affairs followed, including one with an executive who reported to him. The board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation on November 11, according to a regulatory filing, and announced it the next morning. Kress became interim chief executive. Jones, who has sat on Nvidia's board since 1993, became its first-ever chairman.
A Campaign From the Top
The push to bring Jensen Huang back drew some of the most powerful voices in business and politics.
Elon Musk said he had signed a petition urging his reinstatement. One ally told the Financial Times they were rallying tech leaders to press the board and seek the White House's support.
President Donald Trump's position shifted. On the day Nvidia announced Jensen Huang's resignation, Trump wrote on Truth Social that "there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple." By Monday, he was telling reporters that he "would not mind" seeing Jensen Huang reinstated, adding: "I think he learned a big lesson."
Not everyone who admires Jensen Huang wanted him back. "Despite pressure from major shareholders we see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO," Dan Ives, one of Wall Street's most prominent Nvidia bulls, told Newsweek on Sunday.
Business, Without Its Builder
On paper, the company Jensen Huang built has rarely looked stronger.
Data center revenue hit a record $107.6 billion. Nvidia forecast $130 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and raised its outlook for the next fiscal year to roughly 75 percent growth, up from 70 percent.
Kress now leads a company whose growth has been bound up with the money it extends to its own customers. On Tuesday, she said the company was "rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees" and noted that "a lot of things have changed over this last quarter."
Charles Elson, a corporate governance expert, told Newsweek that the principle at stake is simple. "No one is above company policy, even the CEO," he said.
Jensen Huang closed his post on Tuesday with a line addressed not to the board or to investors, but to his family: "I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours."
Kress closed the call with a line for everyone else. "Our momentum is real," she said. "Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We've got this."
Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Steven Frank and Edward T. Cummins

sources.news_title: Nvidia enters the post-Jensen Huang era with a bang
sources.text:
Nvidia delivered a message with its first earnings report under new leadership: The sky isn’t falling.
With a new CEO and board chair just days after the resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang, the company reported results Tuesday that beat analysts’ expectations for AI chip sales. Nvidia’s new leaders also appeared to calm some investors’ nerves about the immediate future of a company at the heart of the AI economy.
Colette Kress, the interim CEO and Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, and Harvey Jones, the newly elected board chair, used the quarterly earnings call to answer many — but not all — of the biggest questions hanging over Nvidia, including who will be running things in the near term.
Just hours before the earnings release, Huang had injected fresh uncertainty into precisely that question when announced that he would be “honored” to return to the job of CEO, if the company’s board decided to bring him back.
At the top of Tuesday’s call, Jones shot down that idea.
“The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” he said.
“While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees, customers, partners and shareholders.”
Following the earnings call, Kress poured even more cold water on the idea of Huang’s return.
“Jensen resigned from his position with Nvidia, and the board accepted his resignation,” she said in an interview with CNBC. “The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen, and that is our statement and what the board has decided to do.”
Huang resigned Thursday after reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a woman believed to be spying for China and another with an executive who reported to him. On Tuesday morning, Huang said he had made “serious mistakes in my personal life.”
Jones said the board would consider both internal and external candidates for CEO and had hired an executive search firm, Heidrick & Struggles, to help with the process.
He also endorsed Kress as interim CEO, saying that she had been “instrumental in executing strategy” and possessed a “deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position.”
Investors responded positively to the earnings report and the call, sending Nvidia’s share price higher by 5% in after-hours trading. Nonetheless, the stock is still trading about 30% below the all-time high it reached last month.
The bullishness on Wall Street was driven in part by the company’s financial results. Revenue for the three months ending Oct. 25 was $115.8 billion — more than double the revenue for the same period a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.68, also more than double a year earlier.
Kress also announced that Nvidia was raising its forecast for future sales from the previous estimate of 70% revenue growth over the next year, up to 75%.
“We are addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers,” she said.
Kress singled out demand coming from the frontier AI companies that are developing new models — such as Anthropic and OpenAI — and said they’d been demanding more chips, “even in the last week.”
This is all despite the headwinds confronting AI chip sales right now, such as China-related export controls, public pushback against data centers and the radioactive politics of AI.
Nvidia’s optimistic guidance was “the most important line in the release,” wrote veteran tech analyst Dan Ives, a managing director at Yorkville Ives consultancy.
“There was a real chance a board five days into an interim CEO would hold back a formal outlook, and instead Kress put a number above the Street,” he wrote in a note to clients, referring to her forecast that exceeded what Wall Street analysts had been expecting. Kress’ guidance “speaks volumes about the backlog she inherited” of demand for Nvidia’s chips.
A few of Kress’ answers to analysts’ questions were less specific, or convincing, than others.
Asked whether incoming Democratic majorities in Congress would slow down AI development next year, she said the industry would need to work together with individual communities and the government.
“We’re always going to be engaged with the government, making sure that we are all aligned in terms of what we see in terms of the future.”
AI and data center companies, she said, will need to ensure that “communities understand the jobs that are going to be newly available.”
But it’s not clear that the promise of future jobs will be enough to turn the tide of public opinion in favor of data centers. Earlier this month, 40 out of the 41 data center ballot initiatives put to voters were rejected.
At another point, Kress was asked about new rules from the Commerce Department restricting the sale of advanced AI chips to several countries that have been major sources of revenue for Nvidia in recent years.
The company would “spend some time studying” the new rules, she said, but she did not believe they would affect overall sales because demand from other customers was so strong.
How long this AI euphoria will last, though, is unclear.
Several large companies have recently announced plans to limit their spending on AI services and tokens, questioning whether the technology is delivering the huge returns it promised.
Meanwhile, the number of individuals who use chatbots is growing but the lion’s share of those users don’t pay for advanced computing power. And polls consistently show that more Americans believe AI’s impact on society will be negative, than think it will be positive.

sources.news_title: "Business As Usual": Nvidia's Interim CEO Amid Jensen Huang Fallout
Nvidia’s stock rises as blowout numbers help ease CEO transition fears
Nvidia Board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO: Chairperson
Nvidia Tops Estimates in First Report Without Jensen Huang
sources.text:
Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday, more than double the total a year earlier and well ahead of Wall Street forecasts, in its first earnings report since co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive. The company guided for $130 billion in fourth-quarter sales, a forecast that includes an extra week on the calendar, and said the outlook assumes no data center compute revenue from China. Shares closed the regular session down 0.44 percent at $155.46, rose more than 4 percent in after-hours trading and opened about 2 percent higher on Wednesday.
The report landed after a rough day for U.S. stocks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 848.75 points, or 1.64 percent, to 50,759.42, the S&P 500 lost 1.03 percent to 7,340.53, its lowest close since July, and the Nasdaq Composite slid 0.74 percent, with all 11 S&P sectors lower. Nvidia's results arrived after the closing bell, so none of that session's move reflected them.
Revenue for the quarter ended Oct. 25 rose 20 percent from the previous quarter and 103 percent from the same period a year ago, when Nvidia reported $57 billion. Analysts polled by FactSet had expected nearly $109 billion. Data center revenue was $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year earlier and 21 percent from the prior quarter, while the company's edge computing segment added $8.2 billion, up 42 percent from a year ago. Non-GAAP earnings were $2.68 per share against expectations of about $2.47 to $2.48, and GAAP earnings were $2.70 per share. GAAP net income was $65.3 billion, up from $31.9 billion a year earlier. Gross margin was 74.8 percent on a GAAP basis, operating cash flow was $48.3 billion and free cash flow was $43.8 billion. Over the first nine months of the fiscal year, revenue has reached $293.7 billion.
Interim Chief Executive Colette Kress, who also remains chief financial officer, said in the results release that "our momentum is real," and credited the rollout of Vera Rubin, the company's newest rack-scale computing platform. Nvidia said the Vera Rubin NVL72 system has shipped and described its production ramp as the fastest in company history, with racks running at customers including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Nebius. On the analyst call, according to CNBC, Kress described the situation inside the company as business as usual and said Nvidia now expects 75 percent growth in the fiscal year ending in January 2028, up from a previous forecast of 70 percent.
The fourth-quarter outlook is $130 billion in revenue, plus or minus 3 percent, a range of about $127.4 billion to $132.6 billion, compared with an analyst consensus of roughly $125.3 billion. The quarter will run 14 weeks rather than the usual 13, which lifts the headline number. Spread across the extra week, $130 billion works out to about $9.3 billion a week, compared with about $8.9 billion a week in the 13-week third quarter, an increase of roughly 4 percent. The company also guided gross margin down to between 71 percent and 72 percent from about 75 percent this quarter, and said GAAP operating expenses should be about $11.0 billion, compared with $9.2 billion in the quarter just reported. The release did not give a reason for the lower margin guidance.
China remains outside the forecast. Nvidia said the outlook assumes no data center compute revenue from China. The backdrop is tightening. On Monday the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced an interim final rule meant to prevent Chinese companies from gaining remote access to advanced AI chips, and Congress is considering broader authority over access to chips hosted in overseas data centers. Sources told CNBC that Nvidia has warned customers the new legislation could expose both them and the company to legal action, and that Nvidia said it would not sell chips to customers who rent more than half of their GPUs to Chinese companies.
The earnings call was also the first public test of how the board intends to handle Huang's departure. Harvey Jones, who was named the company's first board chair when Huang resigned on Nov. 12, joined the call and said the board does not intend to bring Huang back as chief executive, and he said the board has full confidence in Kress. A source familiar with the board's thinking told CBS News the board is against reinstatement. The question had not gone away. Employees and supporters circulated a petition that, according to reports, had passed 160,000 signatures by Monday, President Donald Trump was reported to have named Apple's Tim Cook as his preference for the job, and Huang himself has said he would be willing to return if the board judged it best for the company. The board has begun a search that will consider internal and external candidates, and Nvidia has not said when it expects to name a permanent chief executive.
Huang stepped down after two weeks of reports about his personal life that grew into a national security question. A newspaper reported on Oct. 29 that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer, was passing information to Beijing and had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. The two are not related. On Nov. 8, the board announced an investigation by independent directors working with outside counsel, and Huang acknowledged to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife. The allegations about espionage come from unnamed U.S. officials cited in news reports, have not been tested in any court, and the Chinese government has denied involvement. The release gave no update on the board's investigation, and no findings have been made public. The reports moved the stock sharply: Nvidia shares dropped more than 9 percent in after-hours trading on Nov. 11 on a report that the board was preparing to act, opened sharply lower on Nov. 12 and pared the decline to about 7 percent, and the company's market value slipped below $4 trillion.
Much remains unestablished. Public reporting has not shown what information, if any, was obtained, whether any Nvidia proprietary information was transferred, or whether export-control violations involving Megaspeed took place. The Justice Department, which does not comment on continuing investigations, is reported to be examining possible export-control violations by Megaspeed, and no charges have been reported against Alice Huang or the company. Investors have also filed a class action lawsuit against Nvidia and Huang over his reported ties.
On Tuesday the board announced its first structural response. Nvidia said it created a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, which will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export-control compliance and global trade risks. The committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, with directors Stephen Neal and John Dabiri as members, and will meet at least quarterly. Nvidia's existing national security and global trade compliance teams will now report to the committee and to Kress on day-to-day operations.
Congress has set dates as well. The chairs of three House committees said Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter have voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews before the House Select Committee on China, the Foreign Affairs Committee and the Intelligence Committee. The chairs said they want answers about Nvidia's role in allowing what they called dangerous Chinese actors to access its most advanced chips and about the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset. Huang is scheduled to appear on Dec. 1 and Teter on Dec. 2. Separately, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., the chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, asked Huang to testify on Dec. 3 and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Dec. 10, and said the committee could issue a subpoena if Huang does not appear voluntarily. A Commerce Department spokesperson said Lutnick had agreed to appear voluntarily.
The results leave two separate questions in view. On demand, the quarter shows little sign of weakening: third-quarter sales were $19.6 billion above the second quarter's $96.2 billion, and the fourth-quarter guidance implies a further rise of about 12 percent. On governance and policy, the picture is less settled, because the company is led by an interim chief who is also its finance chief, its former chief executive is under congressional and board scrutiny, and the Commerce Department is tightening rules on a market that Nvidia has already written out of its forecast.
Nvidia returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter, including $6.0 billion in dividends. The board approved a $150 billion increase to the share repurchase authorization in September, and about $227.3 billion remains. The next quarterly dividend, $0.25 a share, is payable on Dec. 23 to shareholders of record on Dec. 2, the day Teter is due on Capitol Hill.

US AI chip giant Nvidia doubled its third-quarter revenue to more than $115 billion (about €104.59 billion), the company said Tuesday.
Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones also confirmed that the board of directors has no plans to bring back former CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang resigned on Thursday after a string of extramarital affairs came to light, including with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
What did Nvidia say about the results and Huang?
In a statement on Tuesday, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" as the firm tries to move on from the Huang affair.
"Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress said in her first remarks since she was appointed last week.
She did not address Huang's resignation or the uncertainty surrounding his successor as Nvidia's CEO.
During an earnings call with Nvidia investors on Tuesday, Chairman Jones said the board had "unanimously accepted" Huang's resignation and "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
Huang pitches return after 'outpouring' of support
The results, which exceeded expectations, were announced hours after Huang said he would be willing to return to the company if the board agreed.
After Huang's resignation, tech industry figures such as Elon Musk, as well as US President Donald Trump, called for Huang to be reinstated as part of a campaign called "Bring Jensen Back."
In a post on X — his first public statement since the scandal plunged the company and AI sector into crisis — Huang acknowledged that he had made "serious mistakes in his personal life" and had failed to "live up to the standards expected of everyone at" the company.
Huang also said he had received an "outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers" for him to return.
Who is Jensen Huang?
Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia, which he led for more than three decades, turning it from a maker of graphics cards used in PC gaming into the dominant supplier of chips driving advanced AI models.
Under his leadership, Nvidia grew into one of the world's biggest — and most strategically important — companies.

Despite the turmoil at Nvidia following the departure of its disgraced founder and CEO Jensen Huang, the company — as expected — delivered a solid quarter on Tuesday. More importantly, Nvidia reassured investors that its streak of record-breaking revenue won’t stop.
On Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim CEO Colette Kress reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from the year-ago quarter and a beat above the company’s guidance. Nvidia had told Wall Street to expect $108 billion in revenue for its third quarter of fiscal 2027. Kress also projected an even bigger fourth quarter, with revenue expected to reach $130 billion, plus or minus 3%.
She also said full-year revenue is on track to exceed expectations.
“We are raising our fiscal year 2028 outlook. We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year over year, up from 70% and off what is now a higher fiscal 2027 base,” Kress said on the quarterly conference call on Tuesday. “Our outlook considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.”
The company also reminded investors that it was using some of its billions in cash to buy back shares. In September 2026, Nvidia increased its share buyback program by $150 billion. It spent $28.1 billion on its own shares during the quarter and still had another $227.3 billion remaining in the kitty for additional repurchases.
Ironically, Nvidia could also benefit from the plunge in its share price following Huang’s resignation last week, should shares remain depressed over the longer term. The stock is down about 10% since his departure. Investors, however, celebrated Tuesday’s quarterly results, sending shares up about 4% in after-hours trading.
Kress stressed that the company was in good shape now and for the foreseeable future, even without Huang at the helm.
“We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress stressed. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.”
She added that the company has secured memory and advanced packaging capacity and is working with its chip manufacturer, TSMC, to “narrow the supply and demand gaps.”

‘Our momentum is real’ – Nvidia smashes Wall Street expectations despite Huang scandal
Nvidia smashed Wall Street expectations on Tuesday evening as the chip giant delivered blockbuster quarterly earnings despite a bruising sell-off triggered by the departure of its founder Jensen Huang.
The world’s leading AI chipmaker reported revenue of $115.8bn (£88bn) for the three months to October, comfortably ahead of analysts’ forecasts of $109.1bn.
The results came as Nvidia’s board confirmed Huang would not return as chief executive, drawing a line under speculation that the company’s founder could be reinstated following his dramatic resignation last week.
Speaking on the earnings call, Nvidia’s chairman said the board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as chief executive”.
Sales surged 103 per cent year on year, while net profit more than doubled to $65.3bn, compared with $31.9bn a year earlier.
Adjusted earnings per share reached $2.68, beating expectations of $2.47, while revenue from its crucial data centre division jumped 110 per cent to $107.6bn.
It marked the 17th consecutive quarter that Nvidia has beaten revenue expectations, according to Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK.
Nvidia also forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130bn, plus or minus three per cent, above Wall Street’s $125.2bn estimate.
The guidance excludes data centre computing revenue from China, where Washington has tightened restrictions on access to advanced American chips.
The results mark interim chief executive Colette Kress’ first major test since Huang resigned last week following allegations of extramarital affairs and links to a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative.
Nvidia shares fell around two per cent ahead of the announcement, extending a sell-off that has wiped roughly a third from the stock’s value since its October peak.
Earnings beat fails to settle leadership questions
“Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” Kress said.
“Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.”
The company confirmed it had begun shipping its latest Vera Rubin AI computing platform, with customers including Microsoft, Google and Coreweave.
Speaking on the earnings call, Kress said the platform had generated nearly $20bn in its first quarter of production shipments, making it the fastest product launch in Nvidia’s history.
But Jacob Bourne, analyst at Emarketer, warned that the earnings beat would not be enough to reassure investors.
“Even a blockbuster earnings beat can’t shift the spotlight away from Nvidia’s leadership crisis,” he said.
“Revenue more than doubled from a year ago, underscoring the strength of its underlying business. But as the company’s first earnings report without Jensen Huang at the helm, concerns will continue to swirl.”
Bourne added that ongoing investigations and uncertainty surrounding Huang’s successor would continue to weigh on investor confidence and the broader AI trade.
Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK, described the results as “a huge beat” with “really, really good numbers across the board”, but warned that the reported SEC investigation was weighing on the stock’s recovery.
Meanwhile, Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, said the figures offered “a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling”.
She cautioned, however, that Nvidia’s forecast decline in gross margins to between 71 and 72 per cent next quarter remained a concern for investors.
Huang said earlier on Tuesday that he would be willing to return as chief executive if requested by Nvidia’s board, although directors have reportedly ruled out reinstating him.
The earnings also come ahead of Anthropic’s anticipated $1.4 trillion stock market debut on Thursday, with the results offering an early indication of whether investors remain willing to back the AI sector’s soaring valuations.

At least that’s the conclusion from analyzing its numbers by conventional metrics. The GPU-maker’s shares peaked on October 5 at $243. At that point, Nvidia sported the world’s biggest market cap at $5.85 trillion. Wall Street analysts following the stock were almost universal even then in acclaiming Nvidia as a cheap stock. And, it appeared, for good reason: Nvidia was selling at 30 times its earnings over the previous four quarters, a modest number for an enterprise growing its bottom line at an annual clip of 100%.
Today, Nvidia looks like a far greater bargain based strictly on the numbers. Since the summit in early October, it’s tumbled 34% as of mid-morning on November 12 to $161, a downdraft that slashed nearly $2 trillion from its valuation, the biggest dollar drop by far, in a condensed period, in the history of capital markets. As a result, Nvidia’s PE has dropped to 20, a figure that given its current stats, tags it as practically the ultimate value play. For example, Apple and Amazon carry a PE of 40 and 22 respectively, and are expanding at a fraction of Nvidia’s speed.
Indeed, despite its immense size and sorcerous growth rate, Nvidia has so far shown no signs of falling victim to the law of large numbers. In the quarter ended October 31, its sales jumped 26% over the previous three-month span, beating the around 20% jumps of the two previous quarters. What about profitability? In the October quarter, gross margins hit a sumptuous 75%, beating its FY 2026 posting of 71.3%.
Make a sober assessment of Nvidia’s overall condition, however, and the best conclusion is that the market is probably right in imposing this giant discount based on Huang’s departure. Nvidia’s wild profitability arises from its virtual monopoly in the top GPU segment. According to a top industry executive who’s an Nvidia customer, it is 18 to 24 months ahead of all-comers in the quality and performance of its top chips. The rub, says this person, is Nvidia’s dependence on Huang as both an unmatched innovator and excellent operator. “Huang was the tech visionary and he also got Nvidia to operate incredibly well,” says this person. “The question is how much depended on Jensen, and how much of what he did can another person do?”
This executive stresses that Nvidia has maintained its huge margins by keeping several paces ahead of the field, and never slowing, one of the greatest feats in the annals of tech. “That continuing advantage in chips is absolutely essential to Nvidia. It’s an industry where you can’t miss a step. If you do, others will catch up fast. Intel fell behind, and it never caught up.”
Plus, competitors who regularly complain about the high cost of Nvidia chips are racing to create their own, in-house competitors, a list that encompasses AMD, Google, and Amazon.
It’s also revealing to parse how Nvidia’s deploying its huge free cash flow to stay in front. In the past four quarters, it’s generated $105 billion in FCF. In the past, it’s channeled a huge portion of that bounty into share buybacks. But in the 12 months ended in October, repurchases fell to just $32 billion. Nvidia’s cash Hoard of $100 billion in relatively modest, and growing slowly.
So where is all the rest of that capex going? Nvidia is famously making big investments in its customers, including SpaceX, CoreWeave, OpenAI, SoftBank’s SB Energy, and Intel (for CPUs). It’s also provided multibillion-dollar credit guarantees for projects built for hyperscalers and neoclouds where it’s providing the GPUs. The practice of funding its own customers is often questioned as “circular financing.” The question is whether Huang felt obliged to follow that course to protect Nvidia’s future. The reason: Locking in future sales as rivals hatch competing products at lower price points. In other words, Huang sought to forestall the commoditization of Nvidia, the threat that’s eventually hit the profitability of all tech hardware giants.
And that’s just the problem. Huge prices and margins inevitably attract cheaper new supply. The market judges that Nvidia’s margins and profit growth will look far lower in the future than in the past, and that losing the genius who could hold commoditization at bay longest was a big, big loss.
A former CEO whom I spoke to took a contrarian stance by arguing that the Nvidia board made a big mistake in not making every attempt to keep Huang. “I would have liked to see more facts, and maybe the board’s got them,” says this person. “The board was not thinking about shareholders. They were thinking about their reputations and not getting sued. They should have punished Huang and made it a very visible punishment like no equity or bonus for a couple of years. They should have found a different way to punish the guy that didn’t damage shareholders.”
This person admits that this is probably a minority view. “People love to get on their high moral horse and that’s what we’re seeing,” says the observer. “You can’t just plug and play to replace someone so critical to the creation of a company’s one-of-a-kind products and operation. A number of CEOs who couldn’t say it publicly would probably say that the Nvidia board forgot what the role of a board should be, to protect shareholders, not themselves.”
That breathtaking, $2 trillion loss in value may be an enduring number, and not just the result of panic selling that most on Wall Street claim.

sources.news_title: Nvidia CEO Resignation Sees Bitcoin Price Fall toward $71,000
sources.text:
Bitcoin slides toward $71K as Nvidia stock tumbles after Huang steps down
Bitcoin fell to its lowest leve since Aug. 20 as tech stocks slid following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Bitcoin (BTC) set new multimonth lows after Thursday’s Wall Street open as selling pressure returned to the US stock market.
Key points:
- Bitcoin price losses hit 3.5% on Thursday as markets reacted to the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
- Nvidia stock fell as low as $148.80 before rebounding to around $160, down 7.2% on the day at the time of writing.
- BTC price analysis sees Friday’s US Producer Price Index (PPI) data as the next key volatility event.
Nvidia appoints interim CEO as stock plummets
Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD dropping below $72,000 for the first time since Aug. 20 as month-to-date losses reached 7.4%.
BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Turmoil at Nvidia following the immediate resignation of CEO Jensen Huang dragged stock markets downward, with NVDA falling nearly 13% at the Wall Street open.
“Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named,” the company stated in a press release.
“The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.”
Nvidia stock one-week chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Economist Mohamed El-Erian described Huang’s resignation as a “significant development” that would have implications beyond Nvidia itself.
“The situation will remain in the spotlight, not only as the company navigates the loss of its highly-influential founder, but also as various political investigations (formal and informal) unfold,” he wrote in an analysis.
Despite the selling pressure on Nvidia’s shares, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index avoided major losses at the open, trading 0.6% lower at the time of writing.
Nasdaq Composite Index one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Analyst looks to PPI release for BTC price cues
BTC/USD fell back below its 21-week simple moving average (SMA), which stood at $73,078 on Wednesday.
BTC/USD one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Assessing near-term macro volatility catalysts beyond Nvidia, Keith Alan, cofounder of crypto trading platform Material Indicators, highlighted Friday’s US Producer Price Index (PPI) release.
On Tuesday, the October print of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) came in above expectations, causing markets to price in more interest-rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.
“Fundamentally, a cool PPI report that lowers the odds of aggressive rate hikes in December/January could easily flip this script bullish,” Alan wrote on X. He added that if the PPI comes in line with market expectations, the spot price could move between nearby patches of exchange order-book liquidity.
The latest data from CoinGlass showed BTC/USD cutting through a patch of bid liquidity as 24-hour crypto liquidations hit $730 million.
BTC liquidation heatmap. Source: CoinGlass

sources.news_title: Billionaire Jensen Huang's Nvidia posts $65.3bn Q3 profit
sources.text:
Table of Contents
Nvidia Corp., the chipmaker co-founded by Taiwanese-American billionaire Jensen Huang, more than doubled its third-quarter profit to $65.3 billion, in its first earnings report since Huang resigned as chief executive over an affair scandal.
Net income for the three months to late October rose 105% from $31.9 billion a year earlier, the Santa Clara, California-based company said on Tuesday, Nov. 17. Revenue climbed 103% to a record $115.8 billion, ahead of the roughly $109 billion analysts had expected and above the company's own August forecast of $108 billion. Earnings were $2.68 a share, against estimates of $2.47.
Data center sales, which include the AI processors that power models built by OpenAI, Anthropic and others, rose 110% to $107.6 billion, or 93% of the total. Hyperscale cloud companies accounted for $60.1 billion of that. Revenue from customers based in mainland China and Hong Kong rose to $11.05 billion.
Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. The outlook assumes no data center sales into China, and interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress said the company will stop selling its H200 chips there.
"Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress said in a statement.
The shares rose almost 4% in late trading after closing down 0.4% at $155.46 in New York. The stock fell for four straight sessions after the scandal broke, and Nvidia lost about $800 billion of market value in the five days after Huang's exit.
No way back for now
Harvey Jones, who became Nvidia's first independent board chairman after Huang left, opened the call with analysts by ruling out Huang's reinstatement and said directors would not take questions on his departure. The board is choosing an executive search firm to find a permanent CEO.
Huang had said earlier on Tuesday that he would be "honored" to return if the board decided it was "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America." In a post on X, he wrote: "I own my mistakes completely. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret." He said he was committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation, which is being run by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.
Before the results, the board set up a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to oversee national security policy, export-control compliance and global trade risk. Nvidia's national security and trade compliance teams will report directly to it.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress on Dec. 1, and general counsel Tim Teter is due to appear on Dec. 2. The hearings follow reports that one of Huang's relationships was with a Chinese businesswoman who has faced U.S. scrutiny over alleged ties to Chinese intelligence.
A shrinking fortune
Huang, 63, resigned as president, chief executive and director on Nov. 12, days after telling staff he had been "unfaithful." He co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and owns about 3.5% of the company, a stake that accounts for almost all of his wealth.
His net worth ended Tuesday at $134.2 billion, down about 16% over six trading sessions, according to Forbes, and more than $50 billion below its peak. The slide has pushed him behind Walmart heirs Jim, Rob and Alice Walton in the global wealth rankings.
Kress, the company's longtime finance chief, has also seen her own Nvidia holding shrink. Her net worth fell to about $900 million, dropping her out of the billionaire ranks.
